issues.legal_issue: A renewed writ petition cannot be used to obtain review of a decision or direction that has already been considered, including after a full hearing.
material_facts: The petitioners again sought review of an earlier decision after an earlier set of review petitions had been dismissed.
The challenged direction to relocate the graves had been made after a full hearing of the affected group.
issues.conclusion: The renewed challenge to the earlier decision and the grave-relocation direction was rejected.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the petitions as a second attempt to obtain review of matters already considered and held that a direction made after a full hearing could not be made the subject of review through these petitions. No statutory provision or earlier case was relied on for this conclusion.

predicates.renewed_review_proceeding: The petitioners brought a further proceeding seeking review of an earlier decision or direction.
predicates.prior_review_attempt_dismissed: An earlier attempt by the petitioners to obtain review of the challenged matter had been dismissed.
predicates.challenged_direction_fully_heard: The court had considered the challenged direction after hearing the affected persons.

issues.definition: When a further review proceeding follows a dismissed review attempt and challenges a direction already considered after a hearing, the renewed review challenge is rejected.

issues.legal_issue: Religious freedoms do not prevent relocation of graves when the relocation is necessary to address recurring violence and maintain public order.
material_facts: The grave-relocation direction concerned graves situated on land belonging to another and placed there contrary to a court injunction.
Religious ceremonies by members of the two sects had repeatedly been accompanied by violence, including stone-throwing, acid attacks, and damage to property.
The violence continued despite the court's efforts to identify alternatives, and suggestions to avoid clashes had been rejected.
Relocating the graves was directed as a lasting measure to reduce the risk of further violence during religious ceremonies.
issues.conclusion: The relocation direction did not violate the religious freedoms asserted by the petitioners; the need to maintain public order justified it.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution protect religious freedoms subject to public order. The Court relied on Section 176(3) of the Code of Criminal Procedure as an example showing that an interred body is not absolutely immune from exhumation. The petitioners invoked V.G. Row's case for a least-interference argument, but the Court concluded that recurring violence and the rejection of alternatives left no adequate less drastic solution.

rule.if: constitutional_rights_challenge and recurring_sectarian_violence and less_restrictive_measures_rejected and grave_relocation_addresses_public_order

predicates.constitutional_rights_challenge: The petitioners challenged a measure affecting religious practice on the ground that it infringed constitutional rights.
predicates.recurring_sectarian_violence: Religious ceremonies by the affected groups had repeatedly been accompanied by violence and damage to life or property.
predicates.less_restrictive_measures_rejected: The affected persons rejected proposed alternatives intended to avoid clashes or reduce interference with their practices.
predicates.grave_relocation_addresses_public_order: The court directed relocation of graves as a measure intended to prevent further disorder during religious ceremonies.

issues.definition: When a constitutional challenge concerns grave relocation, recurring sectarian violence exists, alternatives have been rejected, and relocation addresses public order, the asserted religious rights do not bar the relocation.

issues.legal_issue: Relocation of graves is not established as religiously prohibited or as desecration where the record identifies no religious text prohibiting necessary relocation.
material_facts: The petitioners argued that moving the graves was contrary to Islamic practice and desecrated the graves.
Counsel for the petitioners could not identify a passage in the Holy Koran prohibiting the relocation of graves.
The religious edict cited by the petitioners prohibited unnecessary relocation, while the Court found that the circumstances gave a reason to relocate the graves.
The record included statements that relocation was not contrary to the Koran and historical instances of graves being moved.
issues.conclusion: The Court rejected the contention that the direction was un-Islamic, contrary to the Koran, or a desecration of the graves.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found no Koranic prohibition on relocating graves and read the cited religious edict's restriction on unnecessary relocation as allowing that relocation may be necessary in some circumstances. It also noted the evidence of historical relocations. No earlier judicial case was relied on for this religious-law conclusion.

predicates.religious_desecration_challenge: The petitioners challenged the relocation as contrary to their religion or as desecrating graves.
predicates.no_scriptural_prohibition_identified: The record did not identify a religious text that prohibited relocating graves.
predicates.relocation_has_a_stated_necessity: The court found a reason for relocation beyond mere convenience, such as addressing a serious public-order problem.

issues.definition: When a religious objection to grave relocation identifies no scriptural prohibition and the relocation has a stated necessity, religious prohibition is not established.
